items.title: The Golden Girls , but in a Camp Cabin
items.description: A t Camp Social , where grown women return to girlhood, friendship has no preamble. Within 15 minutes of meeting eight of the campers from Cabin 3, I learned this: In their 50s and 60s, they have no use for the menstrual discs in the camp swag bag; one of them found online dating so depressing after her divorce that she’s given up entirely; when they laugh, they pee a little; they feel like they’ve known one another for years, even though most of them met last night. The campers signed up for this weekend-long adult summer camp for exactly this purpose—to make new friends. On August 21, more than 400 women, some as young as 21, some older than 80, arrived at what usually is a children’s sleepaway camp in the Poconos to spend the weekend bunking in twin beds in log cabins, climbing the ropes course, developing middle-school-level inside jokes, making friendship bracelets, and performing choreographed dances at the flagpole to Cher’s “Believe” and Shania Twain’s “Man! I Feel Like a Woman!” Everyone at Camp Social, regardless of age, is referred to as a “girl.” The camp promises to re-create a childhood experience so that grown-ups can bond with one another as easily as they might have as kids. I signed myself up because I wanted to know what kinds of adults would go back to summer camp and how seriously they would take it. Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic My new home for the weekend with more than 400 possible friends-to-be The girls of Cabin 3 were all in. When they were younger, they told me, making friends did feel more straightforward. But then they got jobs that kept them late at the office, or their kids grew up, or they stopped drinking, and the friendships they’d made with other parents or neighbors faded. They began wondering: How do you meet new people? Where do you go? None of these women ever really thought they’d end up at an adult summer camp, but they saw ads for it and thought, Maybe I’ll give that a try . Which is how they found themselves at breakfast in the mess hall, cross-talking at Gilmore Girls speed, comparing notes on their adult sons, laughing when one revealed her favorite prank—taking a picture of her cleavage on the disposable cameras passed out at weddings. Over the hollering, Jackie Prendergast, a retiree who smiles so wide she shows both rows of teeth, told me that Cabin 3 had decided that its mascot for the weekend would be the flamingo. When a flamingo loses essential nutrients, as it does when reproducing, the pigment begins to drain from its feathers. With time and nourishment, though, the pink returns. “We’ve lost our color, but we’re going to get it back,” Jackie said. Ten minutes later, we headed to archery. Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic The vibes were, indeed, good. T he night before , Camp Social’s girls had gathered in the barn for a dance where a band (all male, all handsome) played Prince, Michael Jackson, and Bruno Mars covers. Liv Schreiber, the camp’s 29-year-old founder, took the stage in her Camp Social shirt. “Welcome to camp!” she shouted, then launched into an ecstatic speech about the weekend ahead. If anyone’s job could be described as “friend maker,” it is Schreiber’s. She is the type of person who skips more than she walks, makes it a point to memorize campers’ names, and, as I witnessed when we met up in New York City before camp, can form a real connection with strangers in a coffee shop in 10 minutes flat. She was working in real estate when she launched a viral matchmaking Instagram account and a matchmaking-party business, which morphed into events for adults to meet new friends. She opened Camp Social in 2023 to relive her own sleepaway-camp experience and to give women a place to meet. The waitlist, she told me, now runs north of 60,000 people. Adult summer camps have been cropping over the past couple of decades—one even dates back to the 1970s—but many of them are co-ed and have the feel of either Club Med in the woods or an all-out bacchanalia. Schreiber’s is one of the only all-female options with an explicit friend-making focus. Bubble letters on the camp bulletin board read You Haven’t Met All The People Who Are Going to Love You ; the camp’s tagline promises that “99% of campers arrive solo and 100% leave as friends.” To get the crowd riled up at that opening camp dance, Schreiber asked, with genuine enthusiasm, “Who wants to meet a new friend?” Hundreds of hands went up. Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic Mornings at the flagpole included choreographed dances to Cher’s “Believe” and Shania Twain’s “Man! I Feel Like a Woman!” That “99% arrive solo” isn’t technically true. Mother-daughter duos and friends arrive together, and returning campers offer wisdom such as: Get to the Soffe-shorts distribution early to get your size, do not miss the Saturday pool party, and be sure to lean back right before the water slide spits you out into the lake. Even so, Schreiber has designed the camp for people to make new connections. Before arrival, campers received a guide titled “How to Camp Social,” which encouraged them to reconnect with their childhood self—the person “who made a friend at the playground in four minutes flat, who didn’t ask if she was too much or not enough.” The camp’s “10-Foot Rule” says that if you’re within 10 feet of another camper, you should smile and say hi. Bunks are grouped by age, but other than that, women are encouraged to make friends outside their generation. The counselors (all female) are trained to be welcoming, Schreiber said. They dance with campers at mealtimes, cheer when someone reaches (or tries to reach) the top of the rock wall, and shout out “Camp Social?!”—a cue for campers to circle their hips and respond with a Kool-Aid-Man-style “Ohhhhh yeaaaahhhh.” Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic The girls of Cabin 3 Who needs this kind of help making friends as an adult? Before I arrived, I’d wondered how many socially anxious people I might meet. Maybe the shyer campers were making themselves scarce, like Cabin 3’s mysterious tenth bunkmate, who kept to herself, or the girl in my cabin who disappeared when we all got ready for Saturday night’s camp disco. But most of the women there seemed capable enough of making friends; they were just in a moment in their life when opportunities to find those relationships felt scarcer. Compared with men, whose friendship skills are more often lamented, women do typically have more friends and are less likely to be severely socially isolated. But having a lot of friends doesn’t necessarily mean that a person’s social needs are getting met, and overall, rates of loneliness between the genders are roughly the same. The women at Camp Social were new mothers, grandmothers, empty nesters, divorcées, widows, and retirees; pretty much everyone was going through some kind of potentially isolating life transition. The average camper that weekend was 39 years old, an age when many people are taking care of kids and aging parents, which doesn’t leave much time for friendship. For some attendees, camp simply functioned as a three-day lake vacation they didn’t have to plan—where they could do yoga on a paddleboard, attend an outdoor screening of The Princess Diaries , and drink signature camp cocktails. Last year, Schreiber told me, one woman in her 80s did nothing but archery the entire weekend. But many of the women I met came in order to feel like girls again, maybe with the hope that that would make friendship feel as easy as it did when they were kids. F or Cabin 3, Camp Social seemed to work a spell of quick intimacy. Of the cabin’s 10 girls, eight of them moved as a pack. (The ninth had come with her daughters and was spending time with them; the tenth I could never track down.) On the way to archery—along the lake and past the cabins, the pickleball courts, the pool, and the ropes course—the girls speculated about how someone would even use those menstrual discs, and Sandi Sullivan, who works for a construction company in Chicago, considered transforming her camp-branded bandana into a halter top for the camp disco, like the one her mom made her in the ’70s. When the archery instructor approached the group, he asked Vicki Petroski, a recent retiree, if she’d be a five—as in the fifth person on the range. “No, I’m a 10,” she replied. The girls cackled. The instructor blushed, and they cackled even louder. (Unlike the counselors, the camp’s staff members—who run the archery range, lifeguard the pool, and referee the camp Olympics—all seemed to be handsome 20-something men with British, New Zealand, or Australian accents.) Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic Jackie Prendergast, a flamingo regaining her color “In my 20s and 30s, I never would have talked so openly with other women I’d just met,” Jackie told me. It helped that Cabin 3 had all reached the age where, as Linda Gryn, a business owner from Pennsylvania, said, “We no longer give a shit.” Some of the girls rarely speak about sex with their friends back home, but here, thanks to Vicki, whose daughter is a sex therapist, somehow every conversation seemed to come back to it. The group was too busy for awkward pauses, anyway. The girls danced: Linda, who had been a majorette in high school and dated a football player, watched the dance instructor like a hawk during morning flagpole routines. They painted (okay, while drinking mimosas) at the paint-and-sip. Vicki went tubing for the first time in about 30 years. “ Everything I did was 30 or 40 years ago,” she said. “When I turned 60, I said, Fuck it, I’m having fun again .” Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic Vicki Petroski and I survived tubing. But being 60 is not always as fun as being 10. At the afternoon pool party, as girls from Cabin 3 and I waved at Vicki, in line for the water slide, Christine—the most reserved in the group, a sensible lawyer with a sensible black bob—came over to me. (She is perhaps so sensible that she asked me not to use her last name.) Going to an adult summer camp at all, let alone by herself, was not usually her speed, she said, and she already has a close group of friends. But recently, the man she’d been with for 40 years “decided he didn’t want to be married to me anymore.” One night, he said “I love you” before bed as usual, and then the next day, he told her, “We’ve had a good run, but I’m ready for the next chapter of my life.” A good run? Christine remembered thinking. I thought that I was happily married . Her adult sons were trying to stay neutral; she was trying to be okay with that. Just then, Vicki went down the slide. The red-and-yellow half tube shot her multiple feet in the air, and we cheered when she emerged from the lake, grinning. Her curls were matted; the purple face paint she put on for camp Olympics was running down her cheeks. Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic The water slide was a hit among campers. Somehow, as the evening set in, everyone still had the energy for karaoke and the disco. The girls in my own cabin, all in their 20s, were getting along well, but if Cabin 3 had reached the peak of camp friendship, my cabin was still in the “friendly roommates who ask about one another’s day” stage. As we got ready to go back out, one bunkmate did my makeup; another, who had been to Camp Social three times, told me the “vibes were off” at the pool party this year because it was overcast. At karaoke, while other bunks performed as a group, we bobbed our heads and drank our alcoholic “Bug Juice,” garnished with gummy worms. Meanwhile, Cabin 3 was on fire. Sandi, whose camp-branded bandana she wore tied up as a headband after all, raged to Smash Mouth’s “All Star.” At the disco, they danced in sequins and jumpsuits to the songs that had been on the charts when Linda was in high school. Then it was Sunday morning and time to go back to real life. Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic “Y.M.C.A.” at the disco B efore the last morning flagpole , campers swapped Instagram handles and phone numbers. People seemed to have made friends, although a couple of younger girls I spoke with told me they definitely had not. They were ashamed that, even in an environment set up for friendship, they hadn’t connected with anybody. Those who had made friends wondered whether they would see them again soon or if they’d be only “camp friends.” When I asked my bunkmates whether they thought they’d stay in touch with anyone, one of them said rather ominously, “Only time will tell.” Nancy Walecki / The Atlantic Goodbye, Camp Social! But over breakfast, the girls of Cabin 3 helped one another download WhatsApp and started a group chat. Since then, they’ve been trading photos of the shirts they had tie-dyed and group pictures from the disco. One of the girls, Jacqui Moore, had painted a flamingo at the paint-and-sip, which has stuck as the group’s symbol. “Keep your pink coming!” Linda wrote in one message. Three girls who live close to one another in Pennsylvania are planning to get lunch. Others might join one bunkmate walking a marathon. (In accordance with their flamingo theme, they say their team name would be “The Flockstars.”) They probably won’t come back to Camp Social, though: The camp served its purpose. Maybe these women will get together annually to share the secrets they can’t with the people they see everyday. Maybe they’ll have a ball at Jacqui’s 60th birthday party. Maybe, like their other friendships, these will fade too. For now, they’re planning a reunion for next year. Greece—or maybe Moab?—could be nice.

items.title: Which Dan Sullivan Will These Dan Sullivans Vote For?
items.description: W hat in the Dan Sullivan is going on in Alaska? Senator Daniel S. Sullivan is running for reelection. Daniel J. Sullivan is one of his challengers. And former Anchorage Mayor Daniel A. Sullivan recently endorsed the senator, while also declaring himself “the OG Dan Sullivan.” “It’s kind of hilarious,” Daniel K. Sullivan, a 33-year-old diesel mechanic and off-road fabricator from Wasilla, who is not running for Senate, told me. “I got a chuckle out of it,” Daniel P. Sullivan, a longtime teacher from Nome, who is also not on the ballot, told me. Control of the Senate could come down to a ranked-choice ballot that currently includes two Dan Sullivans (the Republican incumbent and the Republican challenger) and one Mary Peltola (a Democrat who was the state’s former at-large congresswoman). Republicans are worried that voters could be confused about which Dan Sullivan to select. Theories abound: Is this some sort of nefarious political plot by the Democrats? Or is it just that there are so many Dan Sullivans in the state that something like this was bound to happen? To get at the question, I reached out to half a dozen Dan Sullivans who appear to live in Alaska. I caught a second Daniel P. Sullivan, this one from Chugiak, while he was driving on a remote gravel road the other day. “The Dan Sullivan thing” has become a common topic of conversation, he told me, and his co-workers call him “the senator.” So many Dan Sullivans live in Alaska that his firearms purchases require a deeper background check. “So I don’t get mistaken for another Dan Sullivan,” he explained. (He said that he’s planning to move next summer so likely won’t vote for either of the Dan Sullivans: “Not really fair to vote when the outcome doesn’t affect me.”) Daniel F. Sullivan, a registered nurse, called me back from Palmer. “I often joke that I’m the real Dan Sullivan, and those are all imposters,” he told me. He said he grew up in New York with another Dan Sullivan in his high school, who was a better student than he was: “My parents would sometimes get honor-roll letters in the mail. I always wondered if his parents got all the bad letters about skipping school.” In Alaska, he found that his name had even greater benefits. A few years back, he had workers out to fix the electronic system in his hot tub, and the bill they promised to send never arrived. “I often wonder if the other Dan Sullivan got the bill,” he said. Whenever he’s part of a group going out to eat, the reservation is in his name in case it prompts VIP treatment. In this election, he said, he’ll probably vote but hasn’t settled on a candidate. “I won’t vote just because it’s a Dan Sullivan,” he said. This is not the first time a ballot has featured multiple Dan Sullivans. In 2014, Dan S. Sullivan was running for Senate for the first time when Dan A. Sullivan, the mayor of Anchorage, was running for lieutenant governor (the Senate bid was successful; the lieutenant-governor one was not). Then, in 2016, the former mayor briefly ran for the state’s other Senate seat. Had he won, both of the state’s U.S. senators would have been named Dan Sullivan. Neither of those Dan Sullivans returned my messages. T he Dan Sullivan who has put the name into the news is Dan J. Sullivan, who lives in Petersburg, a small fishing village on an island where Sitka black-tailed deer outnumber the roughly 3,000 people. His father was named Dan Sullivan. So was his grandfather. At the moment, so is one of his sitting senators. Shortly before the June 1 deadline, he filed paperwork declaring his candidacy. “We need a Sullivan who stands up for Alaska,” his website says. [ Read: Republicans have only themselves to blame for their Alaskan defeat ] The only Dan Sullivans he personally knows, he told me in an email, are in his own family: three Dan Sullivans and four more Dans who are not Sullivans. “We all have nicknames,” he said. “Mine will never be divulged.” He says that his campaign strategy mostly consists of maintaining his website and posting on social media. “Maybe some travel, but I don’t have much money,” he told me. (He has $8,400 cash on hand in his campaign account. The other Dan Sullivan has nearly $7.3 million.) His candidacy was immediately challenged by the National Republican Senatorial Committee, which referred to him as “Sham Candidate Sullivan,” and the Alaska Republican Party. Senator Dan Sullivan told reporters in Washington that it was “an insult” and that the challenger was “trying to trick my constituents to rig the election for Peltola.” “This is serious stuff,” he told CNN . “When people are going, Oh there’s two Dan Sullivans, isn’t that funny? No. It’s cheating.” The senator and his allies pointed to similarities between the challenger’s logo and the senator’s: Both are navy and mustard-yellow and feature at least one gold star. They accused the other Dan Sullivan of being part of a partisan plot engineered by a Democratic consultant. The Sullivan facing those questions told me the consultant had helped set up his campaign site and provided “tips on communications and basic campaign functions,” but said “she is not currently working for me.” They questioned his party affiliation. (He was previously a member of the Alaska Independence Party, but when that disbanded late last year, he switched his affiliation to the Republican Party, which he said was in line with his conservative views.) The director of the Alaska Division of Elections, which is overseen by the state’s Republican lieutenant governor, determined in June that the newcomer’s declaration as a candidate was invalid because it had been “filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.” The Sullivan in question appealed to the Alaska Superior Court. “I am running because I am tired of sitting back and watching our current Senator routinely fail to represent the interests of ordinary Alaskans like me,” he wrote in his defense. “The fact that Senator Sullivan shares my first and last names adds insult to injury, motivating me to raise my hand as an alternative choice for Alaskans.” Ultimately, the court determined that Dan Sullivan met all the requirements for making the ballot: It was his actual name; he did live in Alaska; he was over the age of 30. The whole experience, he told me, has been “daunting” because he feels unfairly singled out. “Typical of Sullivan to cry about it, make a nickname, and blame others,” he said, when asked about being called a “sham” candidate. Of the dozens of candidates running statewide in Alaska, he said, “only I have been accused of bad intentions (including one guy who is in jail). Seems unfair to me.” Both Dan Sullivans were on the ballot in the nonpartisan primary earlier this month, after which the top four candidates advanced to the general election. Peltola, the Democratic candidate, got the most votes, leading the incumbent Sullivan by seven percentage points. Daniel J. Sullivan came in a distant third with 2.5 percent of the vote, qualifying him for the general election—and showing that he could be a spoiler in November. His advancement angered Republicans, including the president. “The Crooked, Radical Left Dumocrats have put up another man named ‘Dan Sullivan,’ and they did this to take Votes away from our Great Senator of the same name,” Donald Trump wrote on social media. Senator Dan Sullivan’s early campaign ads have not mentioned the other Dan Sullivan, and when he talks in his speeches about an opponent, he references only Peltola. [ Read: Democrats’ great Alaskan hope ] But this is not the first time an election has featured similarly named candidates and accusations of political shenanigans. When John F. Kennedy ran for Congress in 1946 against a Boston city council member named Joe Russo, his allies helped recruit a janitor named Joe Russo to also run. In 2004, Representative José E. Serrano of New York was primaried by an unemployed former dockworker, Jose E. Serrano, who dropped out after being questioned about his legislative platform and not knowing what that was. In 2024, the governor’s race in Washington State featured Attorney General Bob Ferguson running against Robert Arthur Ferguson and Robert Benjamin Ferguson (the latter two Fergusons withdrew from the primary before ballots were printed). T he name Dan Sullivan is common enough. There was the offensive lineman for the Baltimore Colts in the 1960s. There was the race-car driver Danny Sullivan, who won the 1985 Indianapolis 500. There’s a theater and film director named Daniel J. Sullivan. Daniel was the ninth-most-common first name and Sullivan was the 107th-most-common last name in the United States in 2020, according to census records. There are nearly 5,300 Dan Sullivans in the country, according to the personal search aggregator Spokeo, and more than two dozen in Alaska. In Anchorage, there’s the Sullivan Arena (named for the city’s longtime mayor, George M. Sullivan, the father of the Dan Sullivan who was the most recent mayor of Anchorage) and Sullivan’s Steakhouse (named after John Sullivan, a 19th-century boxer). “Sullivan just seems to be the big thing,” Dan Sullivan the Wasilla mechanic told me. “But I don’t know any benefits from it that I’m aware of. I don’t get any discount at the steakhouse or anything.” The Dan Sullivan from Nome told me he would occasionally get random calls from people around the state confronting him about his campaign promises, especially when the Anchorage mayor and the U.S. senator were both Dan Sullivans. “I’d show my credit card, and they’d look at me and do a double take,” he said. “I got to meet all the Dan Sullivans. All the famous ones. I’m probably the least interesting out of all of them.” (He has since retired and has been traveling, and says he has not yet done his homework on which candidate he’ll support in the election). For the Dan Sullivans, it can be a little disorienting when the political ads are blanketing the airwaves. “It’ll say, Dan Sullivan’s ruining the Alaska fisheries! Or Dan Sullivan voted to raise your health insurance! I’m like, No, I didn’t! It wasn’t me ,” said Dan Sullivan the mechanic. “Or you’ll get an ad on the radio and it’s like, Dan Sullivan’s great for Alaska! Yeah, he is.” He’s not much into politics, so he says he’s unlikely to join the other Dan Sullivans in campaigning. He’s more conservative, so he plans to vote for the incumbent senator. As if things couldn’t get more confusing, there’s also a Dan Sullivan who has run for Congress in Massachusetts. There are so many Dan Sullivans that, at times, my attempts to reach the ones in Alaska went awry. I messaged a Dan Sullivan I thought for sure was from Palmer, Alaska, but instead located one in Cleveland, Ohio. He politely responded that his origins are in Brooklyn and Massachusetts. “I am Daniel M. Sullivan. My dad was Daniel P. Sullivan,” he said. Although he won’t be voting in Alaska, the intrigue has caught his eye: “I have been following this story with interest.” The Alaska race will be determined in November. At least in this election cycle, there’s room for only one Dan Sullivan in the Senate (and possibly none). But some other Dan Sullivans are getting ideas about future options. “Maybe one of us needs to run for president,” Dan Sullivan the mechanic told me. Or perhaps two? “You can pick anybody you want. As long as it’s Dan Sullivan.”

items.title: This El Niño Will Be Unlike Any in the Past Eight Decades
items.description: In the middle of the Pacific Ocean, along the equator, scientists have drawn a box. It’s a big box, two-thirds the size of China, yet hardly anyone lives inside it. This rectangular swath of open ocean is monitored by satellites and a network of moored buoys that measure minute changes in the temperature of the water, with an eye toward anomalies. Every few years or so, driven by changing winds and currents, the water temperature in this part of the ocean starts to rise; even a half degree Celsius above normal over months warrants a designation that an El Niño phase has begun. That’s enough warming to unleash floods and fires, drought and famine, around the world. The box is called Niño 3.4. Right now, it’s hot in the box. “Like a baby pool,” Kristina Tietjen, who spent most of August scuba diving in the middle of this mass of abnormally warm water, told me. Tietjen has been coming to the world’s largest atoll, Kiritimati, for more than a decade to study its coral reefs. She usually dives in a medium-weight wetsuit; this trip, her team needed only rash guards. It is still early in this El Niño cycle—which is likely to be the strongest ever recorded—but the waters around Kiritimati have already been 3 to 4 degrees Celsius above normal. Tietjen’s time on Kiritimati (pronounced like Christmas ) has allowed her to watch, in brutal detail, what these repeated warm-water cycles, playing out in a steadily warming ocean, mean for the great tropical coral reefs here, which were once near pristine. During her first El Niño, in 2015–16, 90 percent of Kiritimati’s coral reef died. Years of slow, partial recovery followed. This month, Tietjen and her colleagues, part of the Canadian scientist Julia Baum’s lab at the University of Victoria, discovered that nearly half of the island’s remaining corals had already bleached—a prelude, if warming persists, to death. When Tietjen comes back, she may well be swimming over a graveyard. Most of the world experiences El Niño’s ripple effects as the heat building up in the equatorial Pacific radiates into the atmosphere and around the globe. This means great gouts of rain in supercharged storms in some places; in other areas, crop-killing dry spells that can extend for months. Along the Pacific Coast of South America, torrential rains and landslides have forced the temporary closure of a main route to Machu Picchu, in Peru; deadly floods have swept through arid regions of northern Chile. Countries such as India and Ethiopia are enduring some of their driest summers on record. El Niños tend to mean more rainfall across the southern United States and drier stretches across a band in the North. Strong El Niños can mean record-breaking heat, and this one is shaping up to be unlike any catalogued in the past eight decades. A 2-degree-Celsius increase in the Niño 3.4 box typically earns the title of “Super El Niño”; we’re already past that threshold, and experts project that the warming could peak at roughly twice as high. “We are now pretty certain this will be an exceptional event,” Malte Stuecker, the director of the International Pacific Research Center at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told me. Part of the reason Stuecker expects this warmth to keep building is that the buoys along the equator can detect water temperatures well below the surface. Down more than 100 meters, an enormous mass of warm water has built up and will rise to the surface in the months ahead. The amount of heat brewing in the ocean has produced one of those graphs in which the current year departs drastically from past trend lines, wriggling up erratically into unfamiliar territory. Although scientists continue to debate the extent to which climate change makes El Niño cycles more frequent or intense, they agree that these cycles are occurring in an ocean that is warmer than it was. Last Saturday, the daily global average sea-surface temperature reached 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit), its highest level on record , according to Europe’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Even if El Niño cycles are not changing at all, as they spiral around that ascending baseline, the temperature peaks they hit keep getting higher, causing repeated blows to marine life and disrupting ecosystems in ways that may be irrevocable. Carlos Zavalaga, the director of the seabird lab at the Universidad Cientifica del Sur, in Lima, began to comprehend the magnitude of this year’s warming in mid-June, when he visited Macabi and Guanape Norte, two islands off the northern coast of Peru. He’d been hearing from colleagues about dead birds washing up by the hundreds on the coasts of Peru and Ecuador. He’s seen the news stories about flocks of hungry Peruvian pelicans swarming the fish markets in port cities looking for food. On the two islands, which just last year were thronged with pelicans, Inca terns, and Humboldt penguins, Zavalaga found empty nests, some with eggs and starving chicks. “They were abandoned islands,” he told me. These seabirds feed on schools of anchovies swept up in the Humboldt current, the cold, nutrient-rich upwelling waters that create bountiful fisheries off South America’s Pacific Coast. During El Niño years, that current gets displaced by warmer waters pushing east across the ocean, and these great schools of feeder fish can vanish from the coasts. The decline has been severe enough that Peru this month shut down an anchovy fishery that is a key economic engine for the country, with much of the year’s quota unfilled. Long before satellite monitoring, Peruvian fishermen noticed these cycles of warmer waters and dwindling fish stocks; they named the phenomenon, which peaked around Christmas, after the Christ child. References to El Niño in Peru’s scientific literature date back to the 19th century. In his three decades studying seabirds, Zavalaga has witnessed die-offs before. But it is the rapid-fire nature of these blows and the severity of the disruptions that make him so concerned. Just three years ago—the same year avian flu killed more than 500,000 seabirds—another El Niño slammed into the coast of Peru. The birds that had made a tenuous recovery since then now face the prospect of another die-off. “It’s like a boxing match: You have a first knockout, you try to recover quickly, and then you have a second knockout,” he said. “I cannot imagine what will be the scenario by the end of this year.” He doubted that the birds could go extinct, but some species might move farther south in search of colder waters. The coastline in Peru and the culture that depends on the fish and the birds could be permanently altered. When the warming started around Kiritimati, one of the few populated islands in the Niño 3.4 monitoring zone, Bill Newton, an island resident, was fascinated by how evident the changes were. He told me that the normally dry island turned sopping wet, and regular floods started washing out the roads. The wet brought swarms of mosquitoes (prior El Niños have led to outbreaks of dengue and chikungunya) but also clouds of dragonflies, which he hadn’t seen before. Higher-than-normal tides poured into seafront homes. Tuna, which can do well in warmer water, attracted dozens of fishing boats off the coast. Prevailing winds changed direction. Corals have a particularly hard time when water warms; they can’t move elsewhere, and they are sensitive to heat stress. As little as four weeks in water just a degree warmer than normal can cause bleaching, the loss of the symbiont algae that supply corals’ food and brilliant colors, according to Baum, whose lab Tietjen works at. Baum, an ecologist, has studied Kiritimati’s reef since 2009. After the El Niño a decade ago killed off nearly the entire reef, Baum began to consider the possibility that she would witness the obliteration of an ecosystem in her lifetime. In a 2018 paper in Science , she projected that successive bleaching events could occur frequently enough that coral reefs, which take roughly 10 to 30 years to recover from mass mortality, would not have time to regrow. In the years since, she had been hopeful that nature could fight back as she watched surviving corals take up symbionts that were more heat resistant. This year’s warming and the pace of bleaching already under way have dispelled that hope. What happens next is in some ways predictable. El Niño is not a haphazard force of destruction; it’s a warming phase in a specific area in the Pacific Ocean that scientists have determined shifts the probabilities for certain weather outcomes in various parts of the world. Those probabilities are reliable enough that, for example, the U.S. Navy already plans to send a hospital ship to the coast of Peru in February to be in position to help after expected floods. But as Baum and other scientists who study and love the delicate ecosystems in the equatorial Pacific are finding, just because El Niño is a familiar cycle doesn’t mean things will be the same when this one is over.

items.title: Iran's supreme leader urges Gulf rulers in written message to unite against, confront 'real enemy'
items.description: Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei urged Muslim countries, particularly those in the Gulf, to unite against what he called their “real enemy” and said divisions among Muslims served the interests of their adversaries. The message was published on Mojtaba’s Telegram account for Islamic Unity Week, which marks the birth anniversary of the Prophet Muhammad (PBUH). It called for Muslim unity, cooperation in various fields and mutual defence, saying anyone who creates divisions among Muslims, “knowingly or unknowingly,” helps Islam’s enemies. “And how, in these times, can anyone attribute such an act to ignorance or negligence, when the tyrants of the world, led by the criminal US, have now cast aside the deceptive and flimsy masks concealing their ugly colonial aims and their hegemonic and domination-seeking schemes, removed their deceptive velvet gloves, and revealed their bloodstained claws to the entire world?” the supreme leader said, according to Iran’s Press TV . He asked whether Palestinians would have been left “so helpless” and “subjected to the oppression and crimes of the occupiers” if Muslims had been united. Mojtaba has not been seen in public since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, in which his father, the previous supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Mojtaba, was assassinated. His call for unity echoes a statement he made on Friday to Iranians, when he said he had banned actions that harm social cohesion and urged authorities to avoid “discouraging statements” that weaken national and public morale. Mojtaba specifically asked Gulf Arab rulers whether “rogues without identity” would have dared to covet their lands and possessions if the peoples and governments of the Gulf had been “united under the flag of Islam.” “My emphatic and repeated recommendation to the rulers of Islamic countries, especially the countries of West Asia and the Gulf, is to identify your real enemy, understand his plan and confront it,” Mojtaba said. Mojtaba, according to Iranian media, said that “unity among Muslims is the fundamental cornerstone for achieving a proud and dominant Islamic civilisation”. “This conceptual and intellectual framework, which embodies our aspirations for the Muslim world, has itself been realised to a considerable extent in our beloved Iran.”

items.title: 3 brothers killed, relative injured in IED blast in Balochistan's Duki: police
items.description: QUETTA: Three brothers were killed and one of their relatives was injured in a blast caused by an improvised explosive device (IED) in the Duki district of Balochistan on Sunday, police said. Duki Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Mansoor Ahmed Buzdar said the blast occurred while a pick-up truck was crossing a seasonal stream near the Killi Bakhtair Khan area of Luni tehsil. “Three brothers and one of their relatives were travelling in a pick-up on their way to their agricultural land in the area when they met the fatal incident,” SSP Buzdar said, adding three brothers were killed on the spot while their relative was injured in the blast. He said the blast was caused by a remote-controlled IED planted by unidentified miscreants. Soon after the blast, police and security personnel reached the site and shifted the bodies and injured to the district headquarters hospital, he said, adding that the pick-up truck was destroyed in the incident. Police said an investigation into the incident was underway. The incident took place against the backdrop of near-constant terrorist activity and lawlessness in Balochistan. On August 27, four terrorists belonging to Fitna-al-Hindustan — the term the state has designated for Balochistan-based groups to highlight India’s role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan — were killed in the Sasool area of Balochistan’s Khuzdar district, the military said. Days earlier, on August 22, a security official embraced martyrdom and six others sustained injuries in a roadside bomb explosion in the Khad Kocha area of the province’s Mastung district. Two days before that, four labourers were killed and three others injured in a blast in Mastung. The incident occurred in the Garo area of the Khud Kocha sub-tehsil — the same area where the provincial home minister Zia Ullah Langove survived an armed attack earlier this month, in which nine people, including six security guards, were injured. The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies’ (PICSS) monthly security assessment said security situation deteriorated most significantly in Balochistan in the country last month. The overall death toll increased by 241 per cent in Balochistan, from 109 in June to 372 in July, the report said. Security personnel deaths in Balochistan increased from six in June to 62 in July, representing a rise of 933pc. Terrorist deaths rose from 75 to 238, while civilian deaths increased by 93pc, from 28 to 54. Eighteen members of peace committees were also killed in the province.

items.title: Filière avicole au Burkina Faso : les vendeurs grossistes d’œufs s’organisent en faîtière pour mieux structurer le marché
items.description: Les vendeurs grossistes d’œufs du Burkina Faso disposent désormais d’une organisation faîtière. L’Union nationale des sociétés coopératives des vendeurs grossistes d’œufs du Burkina Faso a été officiellement mise en place ce 29 août 2026, avec l’installation d’un bureau de huit membres présidé par Salif Ouédraogo. L’initiative vise notamment à mieux organiser la commercialisation des œufs et à contribuer à réduire les ruptures sur le marché national. Dans les marchés et les points de vente, les œufs font partie des produits régulièrement recherchés par les ménages, les restaurants et les petits commerces. Derrière cette disponibilité apparente se trouve pourtant toute une chaîne, allant de l’élevage des volailles à la commercialisation. C’est sur ce dernier maillon que les vendeurs grossistes entendent désormais davantage s'organiser. « Seul, on va vite, mais ensemble, on va loin » , a expliqué Salif Ouédraogo pour justifier la création de l’Union. Selon lui, cette organisation doit permettre aux acteurs de mieux se connaître, de travailler dans la clarté et de défendre leurs intérêts tout en contribuant aux besoins des familles et du pays. Une organisation pour éviter les ruptures L’Union compte environ 100 membres, selon son président. Huit d’entre eux composent le bureau installé à l’issue de l’Assemblée générale constitutive. Pour Salif Ouédraogo, l’organisation des vendeurs grossistes doit également avoir des effets sur l’ensemble de la chaîne de valeur. Il estime qu’une meilleure commercialisation pourrait encourager les aviculteurs à accroître leur production et permettre ainsi de disposer de davantage d’œufs sur le marché. « Ceux qui élèvent les poulets pourront être encouragés à élever davantage afin que nous ayons davantage d’œufs à vendre, pour qu’il n’y ait plus de rupture d’œufs au Burkina Faso » , a-t-il déclaré. La question des prix constitue également l’un des enjeux mis en avant au cours de la rencontre. Le président de l’Union estime que la hausse des prix est notamment liée à l’insuffisance de l’offre. « Le manque qui crée l’élévation des prix » , a-t-il soutenu, en considérant que les difficultés de commercialisation ont, par le passé, pu limiter l’intérêt des producteurs à investir davantage dans la production. L’objectif du « zéro importation » La création de cette organisation est également perçue favorablement par Dasmané Traoré, défenseur des droits des consommateurs. Selon lui, les vendeurs grossistes occupent une place importante dans la distribution des œufs et leur meilleure organisation peut faciliter l’écoulement de la production avicole. « Les grossistes-vendeurs aujourd’hui sont incontournables dans la distribution des œufs au niveau du Burkina Faso » , a-t-il déclaré. Pour le défenseur des consommateurs, une meilleure circulation des œufs entre producteurs et commerçants peut contribuer à réduire les risques de mévente chez les aviculteurs et, à terme, favoriser une hausse de la production nationale. Il défend ainsi une ambition plus large qui est de réduire progressivement la dépendance aux importations d’œufs et tendre vers le « zéro importation ». « L’objectif final, c’est arriver de sorte à booster cette production pour qu’elle soit véritablement suffisante pour combler le vide qu’il y a aujourd’hui et tendre vers le zéro importation » , a-t-il expliqué. Dasmané Traoré estime par ailleurs que l’organisation collective donnera aux vendeurs grossistes un interlocuteur capable de porter leurs préoccupations auprès des autorités. Il a également évoqué les saisies récentes de produits importés et les interrogations liées, selon lui, à la qualité de certains de ces produits. Au-delà de la création d’une structure professionnelle, la nouvelle Union entend donc se positionner sur des questions qui concernent directement le consommateur à savoir, la disponibilité des œufs, leur prix et leur origine. Reste désormais à voir comment cette organisation traduira ses ambitions en actions concrètes auprès des producteurs et sur les marchés. Pour les ménages, l’enjeu sera surtout de voir si une meilleure structuration de la commercialisation peut effectivement contribuer à rendre les œufs plus disponibles et à limiter les fluctuations de leurs prix. Josué TIENDREBEOGO Faso7 L’article Filière avicole au Burkina Faso : les vendeurs grossistes d’œufs s’organisent en faîtière pour mieux structurer le marché est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Koulsé/Coopération : la Belgique prône « une diplomatie de l’action » au service des populations
items.description: BURKINA – BELGIQUE – COOPERATION – RESILIENCE – CHANGEMENTS – CLIMATIQUES Koulsé/Coopération : la Belgique prône « une diplomatie de l’action » au service des populations Korsimoro, 27 août 2026 (AIB) – Le vice-Premier ministre et ministre belge des Affaires étrangères, des Affaires européennes et de la Coopération au développement, Maxime Prévot, a réaffirmé, jeudi à Korsimoro, la volonté de la Belgique de poursuivre une coopération fondée sur des résultats concrets, à l’issue d’une visite de terrain consacrée à plusieurs projets soutenus au profit des populations de la région des Koulsé. Conduite par M. Prévot, la délégation belge, qui comprenait notamment l’ambassadeur de Belgique au Burkina Faso, Erwin De Wandel, et l’ambassadeur du Burkina Faso auprès du Royaume de Belgique, Léopold Bounkoungou, a visité plusieurs réalisations dans les domaines de l’agroécologie, de la santé et du relèvement au profit des populations de la région des Koulsé, notamment dans les communes de Korsimoro et de Kaya. Sous la conduite de la gouverneure par intérim de la région des Koulsé, Bernadette Adenyo/Sermé, et en présence de représentants des partenaires de mise en œuvre, la délégation a successivement visité une ferme agroécologique intégrée à Korsimoro, le centre médical du secteur 1 de Kaya, un site de personnes déplacées internes ainsi qu’un centre de formation. À l’issue de la visite de ces réalisations soutenues par la coopération belge dans le cadre d’un projet de renforcement de la résilience des ménages vulnérables face aux effets du changement climatique, le chef de la diplomatie belge s’est dit satisfait des résultats enregistrés sur le terrain. « On est au rendez-vous de la solidarité selon plusieurs axes », a résumé Maxime Prévot, assurant que les populations burkinabè peuvent « compter sur la coopération de la Belgique » pour poursuivre les efforts engagés. « Ce que je veux, c’est une coopération internationale de résultats, pas juste des grands discours. Il faut une diplomatie de l’action », a déclaré Maxime Prévot. Il a assuré que son pays poursuivra son accompagnement du Burkina Faso, en mettant l’accent sur les priorités définies par les autorités burkinabè. « Notre volonté, c’est d’être des partenaires qui appuient les priorités définies par les autorités burkinabè », a-t-il affirmé, insistant sur la nécessité d’assurer l’efficacité et le suivi des actions financées. Selon lui, la Belgique, partenaire du Burkina Faso depuis plusieurs décennies, prépare une nouvelle programmation de coopération. Une enveloppe d’environ 40 millions d’euros est déjà réservée à un programme de coopération spécifique avec le Burkina Faso, a-t-il indiqué, évoquant également 51 millions d’euros mobilisés en faveur de projets directs portés notamment par des ONG, en plus de l’assistance humanitaire. Pour la gouverneure par intérim des Koulsé, la ferme agroécologique intégrée de Korsimoro constitue un investissement structurant à fort impact pour les communautés locales. « Ce sont de grosses réalisations qui permettent à ces acteurs de pouvoir produire en toute saison. Ce sont des investissements structurants de ce genre que le gouvernement attend », a souligné Bernadette Adenyo/Sermé. Agence d’Information du Burkina ZO/aio/ata

items.title: Le RNI défend son bilan et met ses concurrents au défi de présenter leurs alternatives
items.description: À l’approche des élections législatives, le Rassemblement national des indépendants (RNI) entend faire de son bilan et de ses engagements futurs les principaux axes de sa campagne. Réunis samedi à Agadir pour présenter les candidats du parti dans la région de Souss-Massa, ses dirigeants ont revendiqué les résultats obtenus depuis leur arrivée au gouvernement. Le parti de la colombe met notamment en avant le soutien direct aux familles, la généralisation de la couverture santé, la revalorisation du salaire minimum ainsi que le doublement des budgets consacrés à la santé et à l’éducation. La mise en œuvre de la nouvelle Charte de l’investissement figure également parmi les chantiers cités par Fatima Zahra Ammor, membre du bureau politique du RNI et ministre du Tourisme, de l’Artisanat et de l’Économie sociale et solidaire. Sur le front du tourisme, la responsable gouvernementale a surtout insisté sur le franchissement du seuil des 20 millions de touristes. « Nous ne sommes pas le premier gouvernement à parler de l’objectif de 20 millions de touristes, mais nous sommes bien le premier à avoir atteint ce chiffre » , a-t-elle affirmé. À Agadir, elle a également mis en avant une dynamique touristique qu’elle juge différente de celle observée il y a cinq ans. Le taux d’occupation des hôtels de la ville est ainsi passé de 50 % en 2021 à 71 % tout au long de l’année. Le RNI veut transformer son bilan en argument électoral Pour Fatima Zahra Ammor, l’expérience gouvernementale a permis au RNI de disposer désormais d’un programme « complet et concret » pour poursuivre cette trajectoire. Le parti revendique un programme articulé autour de trois engagements et de douze mesures. Le premier porte sur la protection durable du pouvoir d’achat, avec une augmentation des aides sociales en fonction de l’évolution des prix. Le deuxième concerne la qualité des services sur l’ensemble du territoire national. Le troisième vise l’inclusion économique, avec notamment l’objectif de ramener le taux de chômage à 9 % à l’horizon 2030. Ce discours de bilan a trouvé un prolongement politique dans l’intervention de Mohamed Chouki, président du RNI. Après une semaine marquée par des échanges particulièrement vifs entre le RNI et le Parti authenticité et modernité (PAM), celui-ci a invité les formations concurrentes à mettre leurs propres propositions sur la table. « Nous attendons toujours les alternatives et les idées pour pouvoir comparer » , a-t-il déclaré, citant notamment l’emploi, les politiques de l’eau, la pérennité de la protection sociale et l’accélération de la mise en œuvre du caractère officiel de l’amazigh. Pour Mohamed Chouki, la confrontation électorale doit porter sur les résultats et les programmes. « Un bilan face à un bilan, un programme face à un programme et un argument face à un argument » , a-t-il résumé, estimant que cette approche est de nature à « élever le niveau de la politique dans le pays » . Le président du RNI a par ailleurs rejeté l’idée que son parti chercherait à présenter son bilan comme étant « au-dessus de tout débat ou de toute critique » . Il entend au contraire le confronter à celui des gouvernements précédents. Le PAM en ligne de mire Sans citer directement le PAM, Mohamed Chouki a également insisté sur ce qui distingue, selon lui, un parti solidement implanté sur le terrain d’une formation qui chercherait à se présenter comme favorite à l’approche des élections.. « Un parti fort n’est pas celui qui attend les élections pour rechercher la gloire, mais celui qui investit pendant des années dans son organisation, sur le terrain, dans la proximité et dans l’écoute » , a-t-il souligné. Le président du RNI a poursuivi en affirmant que son parti « n’est pas un ensemble de noms réunis autour d’une échéance électorale » , mais une formation qui « investit dans ses militants et construit ses programmes » . Cette séquence intervient dans un contexte marqué par les spéculations suscitées par l’arrivée de Fouzi Lekjaa, président de la Fédération royale marocaine de football et ministre délégué chargé du Budget, au sein du PAM. Son ralliement a alimenté des commentaires sur les ambitions de la formation du tracteur en vue de la prochaine majorité gouvernementale. Mohamed Chouki a, dans ce contexte, adressé un message à ceux qui chercheraient déjà à se présenter comme les futurs vainqueurs. « Personne, quel que soit son statut politique, ne peut se présenter en vainqueur avant que le citoyen n’ait dit son mot » , a-t-il lancé. Il s’est toutefois dit favorable à une critique politique objective, y compris lorsqu’elle vise un ministre ou le chef du gouvernement. « Les Marocains savent faire la différence entre ceux qui veulent arriver en tête par leurs réalisations et ceux qui cherchent seulement à se donner une image de vainqueur » , a-t-il ajouté. Femmes et jeunes au cœur du discours du RNI Le meeting d’Agadir a également été une occasion pour le RNI de mettre en avant son discours en direction des femmes et des jeunes. Zakia Driouech, secrétaire d’État chargée de la Pêche maritime et tête de liste régionale du parti pour Souss-Massa, a notamment insisté sur le rôle de la région dans les grandes stratégies sectorielles. Elle a rappelé que c’est depuis Agadir que le roi Mohammed VI avait donné le coup d’envoi de la stratégie Halieutis, soulignant le travail mené depuis dans le secteur de la pêche aux côtés des femmes et des hommes de la région. Zakia Driouech a notamment cité la création de coopératives féminines et d’associations, ainsi que l’accompagnement des femmes travaillant dans les unités de valorisation des produits de la mer. Elle a également évoqué sa tournée auprès des militants du parti dans la région, au cours de laquelle elle dit avoir constaté l’engagement de nombreuses femmes. Elle a notamment fait état de la participation de jeunes femmes âgées de 18 à 20 ans venues des zones montagneuses pour assister à la rencontre de Taroudant, évoquant leur « enthousiasme » et leur « confiance dans le parti ». S’adressant plus largement aux femmes de Souss-Massa, la responsable a estimé qu’elles disposent aujourd’hui « de toutes les compétences nécessaires pour contribuer à la création de richesses sur les plans économique et social ». Elle a également insisté sur leur présence dans les institutions, qu’elle considère comme « une véritable force pour défendre les enjeux de la région ». Aux jeunes, Zakia Driouech a enfin adressé un message qui résume l’un des axes du discours électoral du RNI : « votre avenir est entre vos mains et notre devoir est de créer les conditions qui vous permettront de réaliser vos objectifs » . The post Le RNI défend son bilan et met ses concurrents au défi de présenter leurs alternatives appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Djibo : La population se mobilise pour le curage des caniveaux et l’assainissement
items.description: Ce samedi 29 août 2026, répondant massivement à l'appel du Président de la Délégation Spéciale, la population de Djibo s'est mobilisée avec un engouement remarquable pour une vaste opération de curage des caniveaux et d'assainissement aux alentours de la ville. Il convient de souligner que cette activité citoyenne n'en est pas à sa première édition : elle s'inscrit dans la continuité des quatre samedis précédents, témoignant de la constance et de la détermination de la population de Djibo dans cette dynamique de reconstruction. Hommes, femmes et jeunes, main dans la main, ont une fois de plus démontré leur attachement à leur cité en participant activement à cette activité citoyenne. Le Président de la Délégation Spéciale, camarade Hubert DRABO, a tenu à féliciter chaleureusement le dynamisme et l'engagement constant de tous les citoyens dans cette œuvre commune de reconstruction de la ville de Djibo. À Djibo, chaque geste citoyen est une pierre posée sur le chemin de notre renaissance commune. Unis dans l'effort, unis dans le vivre-ensemble : c'est ainsi que nous bâtissons, ensemble, la Djibo de demain !

items.title: Africa’s Road to LA28 begins as Ghana’s Paralympic committee steps up preparations
items.description: Ghana’s National Paralympic Committee (NPC Ghana) has begun detailed preparations for the 2028 Paralympic Games in Los Angeles, with President Samson Deen urging African Paralympic bodies to plan every aspect of an athlete’s journey well before the Games. NPC Ghana took part in the LA28 National Paralympic Committee Open Days in Los Angeles from 25 to 27 August, where officials examined issues including entry documentation, accommodation, accessibility, transport, ticketing, ceremonies and media coordination. The delegation was led by NPC Ghana president Samson Deen and included Foster Kwarteng. The 2028 Paralympic Games are scheduled to take place from 15 to 27 August, with Los Angeles set to host the Paralympics for the first time. For African National Paralympic Committees, Mr Deen said preparation should extend beyond athlete qualification and training. “Our responsibility is to protect the athlete’s full journey. Qualification and training must be matched by early planning for entry, accessibility, accommodation, transport, information and family support.” He said the Los Angeles meetings had helped NPC Ghana bring several outstanding issues into a single readiness plan, while identifying areas where written clarification was still required. Accessibility was one of the main issues discussed during the three-day engagement. Sessions covered accessible operations at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), accommodation requirements for athletes with mobility, visual and auditory needs, accessible ticketing and companion access, as well as transport arrangements for ceremonies and competition venues. Presenters said the layout and fixed curbside arrangements at LAX could require multiple loading zones for accessible arrivals. NPC Ghana says it will seek further clarification on arrival assistance, accessible transfers, mobility equipment and the movement of delegations before the Games. Mr Deen said accessibility must be considered as a complete chain rather than focusing only on competition venues. “A world-class venue cannot compensate for an inaccessible transfer, an incorrect room specification or information that does not reach the person who needs it,” he said. The Open Days also provided information on the Accommodation Management System, which is expected to cover requests, allocations, agreements and rooming lists. NPCs were advised to provide precise information about accessible-room requirements. However, some accommodation allocations, hotel inventories and capacity for additional team officials remain subject to confirmation. Discussions on ticketing covered digital tickets, accessible seating, companion access and athlete ticket programmes. NPC Ghana stressed that any deadlines, ticket allocations or entitlements discussed during stakeholder sessions should be confirmed through official LA28 communications before being treated as final. Entry documentation was another major area of discussion. NPC Ghana said athletes, officials and other members of delegations must obtain the appropriate US visa or travel authorisation based on their nationality and the purpose of their visit. The committee stressed that Games accreditation does not replace a passport, visa or other required travel authorisation. “Accreditation does not replace a passport, visa or other required travel authorisation,” Mr Deen said. The delegation was also briefed on VisaLink, described as a mechanism for coordinating Games stakeholders with relevant visa processes. NPC Ghana emphasised that VisaLink is not a visa, passport, ESTA approval or entry permit and does not guarantee visa appointments, visa issuance or admission into the United States. Admission to the US remains subject to the relevant authorities, including US Customs and Border Protection. NPC Ghana is also working on arrangements for Ghanaian media representatives who intend to cover the Games. Media representatives seeking coordination through NPC Ghana are expected to complete the committee’s media coordination process as well as the relevant LA28 accreditation submission. The committee stressed that submitting an application does not guarantee accreditation and that successful applicants must still meet all applicable US entry requirements. NPC Ghana also says it will limit the collection and circulation of sensitive personal information during the accreditation and visa-coordination process. Beyond Games logistics, NPC Ghana also explored the possibility of a Ghana-focused activation in Los Angeles during the Games. A City of Los Angeles presentation identified Baldwin Hills Crenshaw as one possible area for future African and Caribbean national activations. However, NPC Ghana says no Ghana House location, budget, permit, transport arrangement, sponsor package or commercial agreement has been confirmed. “A Ghana-focused host-city activation is an exploratory opportunity,” Mr Deen said. “Site, budget, permits, accessibility, transport and partner rights require due diligence and written confirmation.” The committee plans to seek further information on possible sites and present the options to the Ghanaian government if it decides to pursue an activation aimed at promoting Ghana through sport, culture and tourism. NPC Ghana says it will now maintain an integrated action tracker covering arrivals, accommodation, accessibility, tickets, ceremonies, media and potential host-city activities. Its Games Planning team is expected to develop a readiness matrix within 14 days, while the Partnerships function will seek a scoping discussion and possible site tour for a Ghana-focused activation later in 2026. The committee says these are internal planning targets and should not be interpreted as official LA28 deadlines. Mr Deen urged other African Paralympic committees to adopt a similar approach. “For African NPCs, readiness begins long before an athlete reaches the start line,” he said. “We must plan the whole journey – from entry documentation and accessible travel to accommodation, transport, information and family support – while verifying every Games-time detail through official channels.” He added that sharing practical lessons across the continent could help African teams arrive in Los Angeles better prepared. The 2028 Paralympics will therefore require preparation not only on the field of play, but also across the many operational challenges that can affect an athlete before they compete. For NPC Ghana, the focus is now on turning those challenges into clearly assigned actions, while ensuring that information is verified and athletes’ needs remain at the centre of preparations.

items.title: Noumbiel : le district sanitaire de Batié tient sa première session du Conseil de santé de l’année 2026.
items.description: BURKINA – NOUMBIEL – SANTE – DISTRICT Noumbiel : le district sanitaire de Batié tient sa première session du Conseil de santé de l'année 2026. Batié, 28 août 2026 (AIB) – Le district sanitaire de Batié a tenu, le jeudi 27 août 2026 à Batié, la première session du Conseil de santé du district. L'objectif est d'examiner l'état de mise en œuvre des recommandations issues de la session précédente, de faire le point sur la situation de la lutte contre le paludisme, d'échanger sur les Journées nationales de lutte antilarvaires, de dresser le bilan des organisations à base communautaire, ainsi que d'envisager des perspectives pour renforcer les interventions sanitaires, afin d'améliorer la qualité des soins. Le Conseil de santé du district (CSD) est un organe consultatif et participatif qui constitue un cadre statutaire de réflexion sur les problématiques majeures de santé et les difficultés de fonctionnement des structures sanitaires, ainsi que de formulation de recommandations pour améliorer la gestion des formations sanitaires. Présidé par le Haut-commissaire de la province, Drissa Hema, le conseil a tenu toute sa promesse avec l'implication de l'ensemble des acteurs, depuis les autorités administratives, coutumières et religieuses, les leaders communautaires, les organisations à base communautaire (OBC), jusqu'à l'équipe cadre du district (ECD). D'entrée, Camarade Drissa Hema a salué le dévouement du personnel de santé et encouragé l'ensemble des acteurs à renforcer la cohésion, la collaboration, le dynamisme et l'engagement collectif afin de mieux répondre aux défis sanitaires. Le Médecin chef du district sanitaire de Batié, Dr Wendnonga Roland Konkobo, a salué un « bilan satisfaisant » au regard d'un certain nombre de facteurs, notamment la lutte contre le paludisme à travers des actions de prévention telles que la pulvérisation intradomiciliaire, la campagne de prévention du paludisme saisonnier, ainsi que les Journées nationales de lutte antilarvaires. À l'issue des échanges, plusieurs recommandations ont été formulées et le Haut-commissaire a souhaité leur mise en œuvre à travers des actions concrètes, afin de renforcer les interventions sanitaires et de garantir une meilleure qualité des soins au profit des populations du Noumbiel. Agence d'information du Burkina HO/ata

items.title: Foods you must eat if you have irregular periods
items.description: The average gap between two periods is around 28 days. If your periods are often delayed by more than a week, then you could be suffering from oligomenorrhea. This is the medical term for the common condition of irregular periods. The causes for irregular periods can be many: thyroid disorders, stress, travel, excessive consumption of alcohol or caffeine, etc. Here are some foods that can help you treat irregular periods. Ginger From getting rid of a cold to improving digestion, ginger seems to be the number one health spice. But this Vitamin C and magnesium-rich food can come to your rescue in case of irregular periods too. If nibbling on ginger is too difficult, indulge in ginger tea every day. It is believed to help stimulate uterine contractions, which may facilitate the onset of menstruation. Adding a little jaggery as a sweetener can make the tea more palatable. Papaya Eating papaya regularly also helps in contracting the uterus muscles. Apart from producing heat in the body, the fruit contains carotene. This substance stimulates or regulates the estrogen hormone levels in the body. Naturally, this induces periods or menses more frequently. No wonder, it is advised to abstain from this fleshy fruit during pregnancy. Pineapple Apart from the shedding of an unfertilised egg, menstrual bleeding mainly occurs when the lining of the uterus is shed. Therefore, foods believed to support the natural shedding of the uterine lining may help promote menstrual flow. Pineapple is one such fruit as it contains the enzyme bromelain. Moreover, this tangy fruit also helps in the generation of red and white blood cells. This implies improved blood flow. Parsley This herb may be very similar to coriander but has slightly different properties. For ages, parsley has been used as an emmenagogue, i.e. a herb that increases the profusion of blood flow in the pelvic area. Don’t forget to include boiled parsley water or parsley tea in your daily liquid diet. Carom seeds Once again, apart from clearing your bowels, this is yet another spice that can work miracles with your menstrual cycle. Gulping down a glass of boiled water with carom seeds helps stimulate the uterus effectively. The best part is that its anti-spasmodic qualities help in preventing menstrual cramps and pains as well. Apart from adopting these effective, easy, and home-based methods, it is always advisable to consult a doctor. Getting medical treatment from an expert as per your unique body type and condition is vital. Moreover, the problem is half solved only when the root cause of the issue is diagnosed.

items.title: Fire engulfs storeroom at Apaaso, Kintampo
items.description: Firefighters from the Kintampo Fire Station have saved a six-bedroom house from extensive damage after fire engulfed its storeroom and began spreading to adjoining rooms at Apaaso in the Kintampo Municipality. According to Facebook post shared by the Ghana National Fire Service on Saturday, August 29, the incident occurred on Monday, August 24, with the Fire Station receiving a running call at 6:21pm reporting the outbreak. A crew of seven, led by ADOII Muriya Gordon, was immediately dispatched in fire tender DPT No. FS498, driven by STNOI Adu Clement. The crew arrived at the scene at 6:32pm and found the storeroom fully engulfed, with flames threatening to spread into the adjacent rooms. Following an assessment, the duty officer ordered the firefighters to commence operations. The team successfully contained the blaze and saved all six rooms of the house. The fire was brought under control at 6:43pm and completely extinguished at 7:03pm. After the operation, firefighters educated the occupants on proper housekeeping and key fire-prevention measures. They also stressed the importance of keeping fire extinguishers in homes and ensuring household members know how to use them effectively.

items.title: Gas tanker accident triggers leak at Fiaso
items.description: A bulk tanker carrying 4,000kg of gas was involved in an accident at Fiaso on the Techiman-Nkoranza Highway on Thursday, August 27, resulting in a leak from the tank. According to a post shared on Facebook by the Ghana National Fire Service, the incident was reported to the fire service at 9:35am, prompting an immediate response from fire crews in Techiman and Nkoranza. DPT FS 547, stationed at Techiman, was dispatched as the base pump with six firefighters, driven by SubO Kusi Collins and commanded by AstnO Awal Mohammed. A second pump, DPT FS 509, from Nkoranza, also arrived with a six-member crew to support the operation. “The incident was reported at 0935hrs on the 27th August, 2026.DPT FS 547 stationed at Techiman with a crew of six(6), driven by SubO Kusi Collins and under the command of AstnO.” Upon arrival at 10:23am, firefighters assessed the tanker and surrounding area before halting vehicular movement on the highway as a precaution. The crews then used foam concentrate to tactically control the situation and successfully stopped the leakage. The Municipal Chief Executive of Nkoranza South, Godfred Dapaa, was present at the scene. No casualties were recorded.

items.title: BCI urges women to prioritise breast health to reduce cancer cases , deaths in Ghana
items.description: Breast Care International (BCI) has urged women to prioritise their breast health as part of efforts to reduce breast cancer cases and deaths in Ghana. According to the organisation, although intensified public education has improved awareness of the disease, more than 5,000 cases are still recorded annually, with about 2,300 women losing their lives. Speaking to the media after a breast cancer sensitisation programme at the Assemblies of God Church at Nsawam in the Eastern Region, President of Breast Care International, Dr Beatrice Wiafe Addai, described the situation as extremely concerning, particularly as breast cancer is treatable when detected early. She said the disease only becomes difficult to treat when it is diagnosed at an advanced stage, urging women to undertake regular self-breast examinations or visit health facilities for routine screening and early detection. “We’re concerned about breast cancer, which is diagnosed among 5,000 Ghanaian women every year and which claims the lives of more than 2,300 of them. This is unacceptable. It’s close to 50 per cent, and that is something that should concern all of us,” she told journalists. Dr Wiafe Addai said the grim statistics have strengthened the organisation’s resolve to ensure that every Ghanaian woman understands breast cancer through sustained awareness creation across the country to tackle the growing challenge. She also thanked Kempinski Hotel Gold Coast City and other partners for their continuous support in championing initiatives aimed at preventing avoidable deaths among women. Dr Wiafe Addai further expressed gratitude to the Assemblies of God Church at Nsawam, particularly the pastor’s wife, for inviting the organisation to educate women in the church and the wider community about breast cancer. A representative of Kempinski Hotel Gold Coast City, Accra, Emelia Naa Nelly, said the initiative formed part of the hotel’s corporate social responsibility efforts to collaborate with Breast Care International to educate women and fight breast cancer. She said the fight against breast cancer forms part of sustained efforts by the two organisations over the years to tackle the disease, stressing that the campaign should not be limited to October but pursued throughout the year. She also urged women to voluntarily undergo regular screening to facilitate early detection and ensure easier treatment and better outcomes. Wife of the Assemblies of God Eastern Region B Superintendent, Princess Asiedu, thanked Dr Beatrice Wiafe Addai and the Peace and Love Hospitals for their commitment to tackling the spread of breast cancer in the area and across the country. She said the awareness programme was significant as it helped participants understand that breast cancer is not necessarily a death sentence when detected early. According to her, the education would encourage women to undergo regular screening to detect and treat the disease at an early stage. Mrs Asiedu also urged married men to support their wives when they contract breast cancer and not abandon them during such difficult periods. Dr Elise Cook, formerly of the American Cancer Society and a volunteer with Breast Care International, said breast cancer deaths remain significantly high in Ghana compared to the United States, underscoring the need to prioritise the fight against the disease. She said the challenge is compounded by the tendency of some women to seek medical attention only when the disease has progressed to an advanced stage. Dr. Cook, therefore, urged women to seek medical attention immediately after noticing any unusual changes, particularly a lump in the breast. “If women were coming to the hospital as soon as they see the breast lump, that would make a huge difference in their lifespan,” she noted.

items.title: Bassitenga/Loumbila : Fin du camp militaro-culturel des adolescents et des jeunes de l’AE de ce
items.description: Bassitenga/Loumbila : Fin du camp militaro-culturel des adolescents et des jeunes de l'AE Loumbila, 27 août 2026 (AIB) – La troisième édition du Camp militaro-culturel des adolescents et des jeunes (CMC-AJ 2026), qui regroupe des campeurs de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES), a pris fin, jeudi 27 août 2026, au Collège de jeunes filles de Loumbila, après huit jours d'activités placées sous le signe du panafricanisme, de la résilience et de l'engagement citoyen. Organisé du 20 au 27 août 2026 par le ministère des Sports, de la Jeunesse et de l'Emploi, le camp avait pour thème : « Jeunesse résiliente et patriote engagée au service de la souveraineté de l'AES ». Durant huit jours, les campeurs ont participé à diverses activités militaires, culturelles, sportives et éducatives visant notamment à renforcer leur discipline, leur résilience, leur esprit patriotique et leur engagement citoyen. Le camarade Alexandre Yougbaré, représentant le ministre à cette cérémonie, a exprimé sa satisfaction quant au déroulement du camp. « Le département en charge du Sport et de la Jeunesse est satisfait, parce que nous avons vu des enfants qui ont une vision. Car sans cette vision, tout le travail que le gouvernement du Burkina Faso et l'ensemble des pays de l'AES sont en train de faire actuellement serait un travail vain », a-t-il indiqué. Il a salué l'engagement et l'assiduité des jeunes tout au long du camp. Il a insisté sur l'importance de telles initiatives dans la formation d'une jeunesse consciente de ses responsabilités et résolument engagée dans la construction d'un espace AES solidaire et souverain. Le directeur du camp, Dr Somaïla Sawadogo, a, de son côté, relevé l'engagement des participants dans les différentes activités programmées. Il les a invités à capitaliser sur les enseignements acquis durant leur séjour et à les mettre au service de leurs communautés respectives. Il rêve de la pérennité de cette belle initiative au profit du plus grand nombre d'adolescents et de jeunes de l'AES. Prenant la parole au nom des participants, la campeuse Aïchatou Abdoul Adamou, venue du Niger, s'est réjouie de sa participation à cette troisième édition. Elle a particulièrement salué les liens de fraternité, d'amitié et de solidarité qui se sont tissés entre les jeunes des pays de l'AES au cours du camp. « Nous avons beaucoup appris sur les différentes cultures présentes au Burkina et au Niger. Nous faisons du sport chaque matin ; le soir, ce sont les pas de danse, la veillée, le journal du camp. Nous avons découvert les métiers de la peinture et de la saponification. Ces activités représentent pour nous un lien de fraternité, de solidarité et aussi de patriotisme, parce que qui dit Burkina dit Niger, dit Mali », a-t-elle ajouté. Cette troisième édition du Camp militaro-culturel des adolescents et des jeunes a ainsi offert un cadre de rencontre, de formation et de partage d'expériences entre les jeunes de l'espace AES. Elle entend contribuer à l'émergence d'une jeunesse davantage consciente des enjeux de souveraineté, de résilience et de développement des pays membres de la Confédération des États du Sahel. Agence d'information du Burkina SO/LC
